column5: faith and patience inheriting the promise
column6: The commentary's exception begins with belief and ends with mutual counsel to sabr; Hebrews urges imitation of those who inherit the promises through faith and patience. This gives the faith-patience pairing a concrete inheritance horizon.

The commentary pairs righteous deeds with patience; Paul describes those who seek glory and immortality through endurance in good work and receive eternal life. It joins ethical action and perseverance in a judgment setting.

column5: mutually spurring love and good works
column6: The commentary says believers repeatedly counsel one another and do righteous deeds; Hebrews asks the community to consider how to stir one another to love and good works. This is a distinct reciprocal-action detail from the encouragement in Hebrews 10:25.

column5: Jeremiah lowered into a cistern to die
column6: The commentary's B002 image is a person held for death; Ebed-Melech says Jeremiah was put in the cistern to die of hunger because no bread remained. The verse supplies an explicit instance of detention with death as its intended outcome.

column5: asking that a sin not be held against killers
column6: The commentary says each soul is held to what it has earned; while being stoned, Stephen asks the Lord not to hold this sin against his killers. The dying victim's plea reverses the image of deeds holding a person liable.

column5: delayed judgment as patience for repentance
column6: The commentary has the prophet wait for the Lord's judgment; Peter says the Lord's apparent delay is patience, allowing people time to reach repentance rather than perish. It makes waiting itself a merciful postponement of loss.

column5: the returning master finds servants watching
column6: The commentary says the one who waits is under observation; Jesus blesses servants whom their returning master finds awake and watching. This gives the watched wait an eschatological household scene and a reward for readiness.

The commentary defines sabr as waiting for the Lord's decree; Habakkuk says the vision has an appointed time and, even if it seems delayed, the hearer must wait for it. It makes delay part of the promise rather than evidence that it failed.

The commentary calls sabr a wait for the Lord's judgment; the psalmist says he waited patiently for the LORD, who inclined to hear his cry. This gives waiting an urgent prayer setting rather than making it a general disposition.

The commentary sets self-restraint beside being held by another; the next verse says the LORD draws the psalmist from a destructive pit and mud. This supplies a specific image of release from confinement, distinct from the preceding verse's patient wait.

The commentary opposes sabr to panic and describes waiting for the Lord's judgment; Lamentations says it is good to wait quietly for the LORD's salvation in the aftermath of Jerusalem's ruin. It gives restrained waiting a voice within communal catastrophe.

column5: God slow to anger after rebellion
column6: The commentary makes patience restraint and waiting for judgment; after Israel's breach, God describes himself as slow to anger and abundant in steadfast love. It adds divine patience as the quality that makes judgment and renewed relationship coexist.

column5: the Lord waits to show grace and blesses those who wait
column6: The commentary has the prophet wait for the Lord's decree and says the waiting person remains in God's sight; Isaiah says the LORD waits to show grace and blesses those who wait for him. The two-sided waiting makes delay a merciful encounter.

The commentary glosses sabr as holding oneself back from panic or outcry; the Talmud praises people who suffer insult without insulting back or replying. Its reading of the lovers of God in Judges 5:31 turns restraint under humiliation into a sign of devotion.

The commentary says humanity is in loss except for those who do righteous deeds; in Jesus' parable the owner reports three years of seeking fruit from a tree that bears none and orders it cut down. It gives fruitlessness a specific scene of impending loss.

column5: delaying the felling for another year
column6: The commentary frames sabr as waiting for the Lord's judgment; in the same parable the gardener asks that the tree be left one more year to be dug around and fertilized. The delay gives the condemned tree time to bear fruit.

column5: reinterpreting apparent loss as hidden good
column6: The commentary presents humanity as being in loss and patience as waiting for God's decree; Rabbi Akiva interprets a chain of setbacks as for the good after those very losses protect his life. This Jewish story preserves trust without pretending the setbacks initially look beneficial.

column5: refusing coerced food at the cost of death
column6: The commentary distinguishes self-restraint from being restrained by another and calls fasting a kind of sabr; Eleazar is pressured to eat forbidden meat but accepts torture rather than violate the law. The martyr narrative makes bodily abstention an act of chosen fidelity under lethal coercion.

column5: waiting for grace rather than immediate judgment
column6: The commentary's waiting sabr is directed toward God's ruling; Isaiah links the Lord's own waiting to grace. This adds the specific reading of divine delay as mercy, distinct from the verse's reciprocal pattern of the Lord and people waiting.
